BRIDGE.	„

1.	Why has the government not gone on with the building of the highway bridge between Hawkesbury, Ontario, and Grenville, Quebec, in pursuance of the vote passed last session ?
2.	Will this work be proceeded with immediately? If not, why not?
3.	Is it intended to build this bridge at the head of the rapids so that it will start right at the village of Grenville on the Quebec side?

This question can be best answered by my giving a memo, furnished me by the deputy minister of my department. That memo, is as follows;
With reference to the bridge across the Ottawa rivgr at Hawkesbury, Ont., the delay in JJim-Unatter has been on account of the approach to the bridge on the Ontario side. It seems that the most favourable site, and the natural crossing point, brings the Ontario end of the bridge to a roadway which runs through the Hawkesbury Lumber Company's property.
Although I do not think there is anything in writing, it has been understood all along, or at least expected, that the town of Hawkesbury would arrange with the Hawkesbury Lumber Company for a right of way through their property giving an approach to the bridge and, I may say, it is the custom for municipalities to do this.
I understand, however, that recently there has been some trouble between the town and the Hawkesbury Lumber Company in regard to the latter's assessment, so that their relations are not now friendly, which will possibly result in the town not proceeding any further in the matter. On account of the difficulty in securing the approach, other locations have been suggested and have been looked into, but, as stated above, the one referred to is the natural crossing.
Preliminary plans showing the exact location of the bridge piers have been prepared and superstructure plans have been adopted.
The most favourable time for proceeding with the work would be following high-water next year, say in June, and if a decision is come to regarding the location and the acquisition of the right of way thereto, detailed plans could be got out and a call for tenders made.

On the 6th day of December last, my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur), in answering paragraph 3 of a question concerning the cruiser ' Niobe ' namely :
Had the 'Rainbow' been scrapped by the imperial authorities at the time of said purchase?
The hon. minister replied ' No '.
My question was founded on the authority of the ' Naval Annual ' of 1907, page 207, in which the statement appears :
The following vessels have been struck off the effective list, but the armaments have not in every case been removed:-
Third-class cruisers-'Andromache,' 'Apollo,' 'Intrepid,' 'Melampus,' 'Naiaid,' 'Pique,' 'Rainbow,' 'Spartan' and 'Tribune,' which were built under the Naval Defence Act.
I presume my hon. friend had not seen that authority when he said that the 'Rainbow ' had not been scrapped.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I do not think the ' Naval Annual ' says that it was scrapped.
I have just quoted my authority.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It does not say that the ship was scrapped so that my hon. friend is absolutely mistaken. The ' Naval Annual ' is not an official publication, and in that book it is not said that the ' Rainbow ' has been scrapped. Besides I may inform my right hon. friend that there are under the Admiralty four lists. One is the royal navy list, the second is the auxiliary list, the third is the harbour list, and there is another which I do not remember. I shall get for my hon. friend all the information regarding that and wall give it in reply to another question he has on the Paper.
Does my hon. friend say that the ' Niobe ' has not been scrapped?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Certainly not ; quite the reverse. It is on the navy list today, as my hon. friend will find if he will consult it. He will also see that in 1907 when the vessel was purchased, it was in the auxiliary list and was carrying its armament, so that it was not scrapped at all.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I might explain to the House that if these purchases were not for departments of the government, it "would be contrary to our usual practice to bring them down, inasmuch as the law requires that the business of individuals is not to be disclosed, this provision being made for very good reasons which one can understand; but I think in this case where the government [DOT] departments are concerned, the return asked for by the hon. gentleman should be given him.

For a statement showing:-1. The names of all those engaged to date by the government in connection with the new Naval Department, whether for service at sea or for work in connection with the department, either for inside or outside 'service.
2.	The domicile of origin of those thus on-gaged, their previous occupation, rank ior grade in the British navy or elsewhere, and previous rate of pay or remuneration.
3.	The duties assigned, rank or occupation of those thus engaged in the service of Canada, and present salary and allowances.
He said: I suppose my hon. friend can supply the information called for by this motion to the House, before the Christmas adjournment. It would be a matter of a couple of days work in the department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I have been reading over the motion and I suppose it would be possible to secure the information in that time.
Because it would be very convenient when we come to vote the estimates upon this particular branch of the service to have all that information before us. It would save the House considerable time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The object of the motion is to acquaint the House with all the names and functions of the new employees we have been obliged, on account of technical qualifications, to secure in England or elsewhere, and to find out exactly their names and what the nature of the engagement is in each case, and by whom they were recommended.
In connection with this question I had intended referring at some length to the situation in this country of those who come here under special engagement to fulfil technical duties. When Commander Roper ar-

rived in this countrv I think he was guilty of considerable indiscretion in his public speaking in regard to the navy. The matter gave rise to some comment at the time/ but nothing of the kind has occurred since, and consequently I do not think it neces-sarv to insist unduly on what might be considered a pardonable offence. But we would like to know from the minister in charge of the department if the same rules that govern other civil servants in regard to discussing publicly political questions, rules that apply to the ordinary native employees, apply also to those who are engaged from England or elsewhere for this special service. Now, the incident is not of great importance, as I said before, because there has been no repetition of the error. But upon his arrival at Quebec Commander Roper gave an interview to a correspondent of ' La Presse,' in which he gave expression to views concerning the government naval project which I would consider, taken apart from all other circumstances, an indiscretion on the part of a public employee. Here in Ottawa he attended a luncheon of the directors of the Central Canada Exhibition, and he seems to haye spoken a great deal too freely there of those public men who have expressed any adverse opinion upon the navy, excepting members of the government and their followers. In a correct report of his speech in the Montreal ' Gazette ' of September 14, 1910, I find the following words :
He deprecated the use of the term ' tin-pot ' as applied to the navy, adding: tin-pot navy is otten, much too often, used, and I hav* been to some trouble to find out the origin of the term, and have come to the conclusion that it is used by some of those people who are in disagreement with the present programme regarding the navy, and I firmly believe that this disagreement arises chiefly through ignorance or want of thought.
Further on he says:
With regard to Canada's share in imperial defence, a large faction only

He calls the party sitting on this side of the House who were opposed to last year's navy programme, as a faction.
"had one aim in view, namely, the presentation of a couple of Dreadnoughts to the mother country. There arose other ideas, but whatever they were, a Dreadnought was invariably included, and so when these people found that the government proposal did not include a Dreadnought, they immediately designated it ' tin pot/ which, I think yoii will agree with me, is a contemptuous term to apply to a service which I sincerely trust and hope will in the near future be looked upon with gratification and pride by every soul who has the honour of calling himself or herself a Canadian citizen, and who is consequently a member of this great empire of ours.
Further on he comes down to details.
In ' Le Devoir/ about twelve days ago, a letter was published. This letter, amongst other things, stated that Mr. Brodeur is badly advised. As I have the honour of being one of the advisers, I am quite ready to inwardly believe the truth of that statement, though I am not for one moment ready to admit it outwardly. But when this letter goes on to definitely state that neither Mr. Brodeur or Ins advisers have considered a certain matter in connection with the navy, then I think it is time to object. How does this writer know what has or has not been considered? He cannot possibly know, and yet he goes and deliberately makes these statements in the press. Why? There can only be one object, and that is to throw disparagement on the navy and everything connected with it, simply because he does not agree with it. The letter is principally composed of inaccuracies which do not deserve answers, but which may be summed up as the imaginative vapourings of a pessimistic soul.
Now, when I reflect that I was the author of that letter I am disposed to think that this is not quite the way in which our public officials should be allowed to speak of men who are engaged in the discussion of political subjects. He states further on:
The chief object for the present, he said, was to train men for the navy. ' The wear and tear of a future naval war/ he added, ' on the human being will be terrific, and in my humble opinion cases will arise where the personnel will be beaten whilst the material is still available/
Also further down:
Now, I hold no brief for the Canadian government, I am talking as a naval officer. The government's policy as regards their navy may be right, or it may be wrong, but this I do say, and say with all the earnestness I can command, that this policy has been framed by the representatives of the people and is now law. Criticise the programme by all means, but do not let that criticism take the form of placing obstacles in the way of the navy and also dragging the navy into party politics.
, Mr. Speaker, these utterances by any other person would not be perhaps objectionable. But if you let them pass unnoticed you will thereby sanction the principle that public servants in this country may publicly criticise in fairly strong language-since it is a question here of ' the vapourings of pessimistic minds '-may criticise at public meetings the utterances of public men, and I have always understood since I have been a member of this House that that is something not to be tolerated. It is easy to see how far one would go if the principle was once introduced. As 1 have said, the matter occurred once only, and I am quite ready to believe that if, as I have reason to suppose, the official was warned by the chief officer of the depart-

ment, there will be no repetition of this error. But I give the case to the House in order to afford my hon. friend the opportunity of reassuring the House upon that point, and stating that all civil servants, whether native or coming from elsewhere, are absolutely upon the same footing in regard to the observance of those admitted rules.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I mav say to my hon. friend in regard to this motion that I will be glad to give instructions to have those papers brought down as . speedily as possible. I do not know how much work they will entail, or how much information the department may possess, but what we have we will produce. My hon. friend has taken the opportunity of this motion to ventilate a grievance which he has against Commander Roper.
You can scarcely call it a grievance.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I thought from what my hon. friend said that he felt "aggrieved at what Commanded Roper had said. It is but perfect justice to Commander Roper to state that he had been very severely attacked by mv hon. friend in an article which he signed.
My hon. friend is quite mistaken; I never made any allusion to him at all, did not know him. I stated that my hon. friend was ill-advised in the choice of his advisers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: My hon. friend thought it fit to attack the officers who have been in charge of the Canadian naval service, and the chief of the staff being Commander Roper, of course, that gentleman felt that those attacks were mainly directed against himself. Commander Roper, I may say, was occupying an important position in Great Britain. He has been there under Lord Charles Beresford for many years, and has proved a very good officer, so I was informed by the officers of the ad-mirality who agreed to loan his services to the Canadian government. When we required an officer to replace Commander Stewart, as chief of the naval staff, the name of Commander Roper was suggested as being an officer who would be loaned to us and who would be a very capable officer and having given very complete satisfaction. This gentleman, I may say to his credit, as soon as he came out to this country, he undertook the important task of advising the government as to how best the organization could be - effected in connection with the Canadian naval service. He has proved to be a very good officer so far. I have never seen anything which could be reproached to him

in connection with the discharge of his official duties. My hon. friend is perhaps, a little to blame. He wants to throw the whole blame upon Commander Roper, but he should take to himself also a very large share of the blame for the occurrence which he has spoken of. Here are men who come out to this country, whose services are loaned to us by the British Admiralty, for the purpose of giving us advice as to the best way of organizing the service, and my hon. friend thinks it advisable to attack them.

My hon. friend must really retract that word. I never attacked any officer, and I believe that when I wrote that article, Commander Roper had not arrived in this country. Any way, I mentioned no name. Why does my hon. friend persist in saying that I attacked him?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: If the word ' attacked ' is too strong, then I will say that he has cast some reflections upon the technical officers of the department. I think he will not deny that. I have not the article under my * hand, but my hon. friend very likely has a copy of it before him, and he must remember that he was rather severe towards this officer.
I deny it totally. I attacked my hon. friend.
Was Commander Roper authorized by the minister to make the statements he did?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I could not authorize
those statements because I did not see them before they were made. I simply want to sate the facts in justice to Commander Roper because he has been publicly censured, and I think it would be only fair to him, to put all the facts before the country. I have now in my hand the article published by my hon. friend. It is entitled:
Are we baffled?
This is what my hon. friend says:
Mr. McKenna has the assistance of the advices of the ' Sea Lords,' four valuable experts who advise him in the direction of the vast department which he presides. Mr. Brodeur seems to lack greatly of wise councillors.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I do not think that is a very polite word to be used toward those officers who come out here and give us their time and advice.
Translate it into English, please.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I think I have a translation which is better than my own translation.
We will take the minister's translation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I am afraid my English is not very good and my translation may not be too good. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) started in his article to .make a comparison between the First Lord of the Admirality and myself, and he says:-
Mr. McKenna is assisted by a council called the sea lords, four scientific experts who advise him in the conduct of this great department over which he presides.	Mr. Brodeur on the other hand seems to be very meagrely supplied with wise advisers.
I think the words in French were a little harder than the words I have just given in English. But there is also another reference to my hon. friend where he gives some figures which show that those who are advising me do- not seem to know very much about their business.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
My hon. friend goes on to speak of the improved Bristols. Here is another quotation:-
What were these alterations or improvements? What were their objects? What was the improved Bristol?
Mr. Brodeur did not care, nor then, neither later. His counsel did not care, neither.
I think that is a somewhat serious reflection.
What is the translation of that, please?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: My hon. friend is giving me a great deal of work.
Well, the minister is paid for it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I will try to translate for my hon. friend. My hon. friend will remember that in the report of the admiralty it was stated that we should build what are called improved Bristols. Then the hon. member for Jacques Cartier says:
What were these modifications -and improvements? On what points were they bearing? What was the improved Bristol? Mr. Brodeur did not pay any attention to it then nor later on, nor did his advisory staff.
My hon. friend goes on to make some statements as to what the improved Bristols were and how important it was that we should take that type, and he says that my advisers did not take the suggestions made by the admiralty. I think the language of my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) is severe, and he seems to direct his attention particularly to Commander Roper.
It would be pretty difficult to discuss any department of government if one is not permitted to use such language as that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I thought the hon. gentleman should have learned more about the subject before attacking these gentlemen who come over here to give us the benefit of their advice and experience.
Does the Minister of Marine and Fisheries approve of the language used by Commander Roper?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: We must put the two things together. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) lays it down as a rule that a member of this House can severely attack an official and that the official must not say anything in return. With that rule I am not prepared to agree absolutely just now. The officers of the civil service are men just like ourselves; they have their opinions, their opinions should be respected, and they should not be unduly criticised. The statement was made that I was provided with a poor naval staff, and Commander Roper of that naval staff naturally resented it. I do not want civil servants to engage in our party warfare, hut at the" same time if civil servants are attacked even by members of parliament why should they not have the right to answer these attacks? I do not know why the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) went out of his way to say these disagreeable things in reference to these new men who came to the country under the circumstances I have described. I as head of the department was responsible for their official conduct and why take them ' a partie.'
Does the minister approve of the conduct of this officer in this instance?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I am stating the facts, and I think it is due to Commander Roper that the facts should be laid before the House. My hon. friend has simply stated what Commander Roper said, but he has not mentioned what provoked it, and I leave the House to judge whether under the circumstances Commander Roper should be blamed. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) had not brought the matter up in the manner in which he did, perhaps the speech of Commander Roper would not have been made. Commander Roper has explained to me that he thought that when he was attacked he had the right to answer, and as a general rule, if members of this House see fit to attack directly civil servants, the civil servants surely should have the right to answer?

I was present at the luncheon of the directors of the Central Canada Exhibition when Commander Roper made his speech. I did not intend to bring the matter up in the House, nor did I know that my hon. friend

(Mr. Monk) intended to bring it up, but I am bound to say that the remarks of Commander Roper went much beyond the scope that has just now been mentioned by the Minister of Marine. I do not want to say anything harsh about Commander Roper. I admit at once that probably some considerable allowance - should be made on account of his being a comparative stranger in Canada and perhaps not thoroughly accustomed to the way in which matters of this kind are managed here.
Or in England either.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I have called Captain Roper s attention to the word ' faction,' he has told me, by way of explanation, that the word has a very different meaning m England from what it has here.

I do not know what meaning may be attributed to that word by Commander Roper, but I regard it as a very unfortunate expression for him to use under the circumstances. He is not concerned in explaining or defending the policy of the department. That is a matter for the minister and the members of the government to deal with. He should not open his mouth on that subject, and the sooner the minister gives him or any other officer in the service To understand that, the better it will be in the interest of the officers themselves and also in the interest of the people of this country.

I was quite surprised when the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) took the ground he did this afternoon. What applies to the civil service in the conduct of his department applies to the civil service generally, and it appears to me that the minister has broken altogether new and altogether dangerous ground in the statements he has made. He has practically stood behind an officer of his department, who made these remarks evidently in reply to a letter which did not name Commander Roper or any other individual member of the service, but which was a criticism of the department itself. In that criticism the statement was made that the minister was poorly advised with reference to certain things. Now the minister stands behind his officer, and gives us to understand that the government also stand behind the position which he assumes. So . that if in this House I or anybody else attacks the Department of Public Works, the Department of Railways and Canals, and savs that the minister has been poorly advised in any undertaking, any officer or subordinate in either of these departments, according to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, has a perfect right to get up on a public platform and launch out into a discussion of policy and a denunciation of the member of parliament who made the criticism. Does the Prime Minister stand behind that doctrine? The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has enunciated it and supported it, and he says in effect that Commander Roper was perfectly justified in alluding to a matter of policy and discussing it in a public place and designating parties and individuals. It would be intolerable if that sort of thing were to be-

come a practice. There could be no such thing as criticism in this House or out of it, except with the contingency of any officer being at perfect liberty to go upon a public platform and designate those who made the criticism in any terms that he thought fitting and effective. I do not believe the Prime Minister stands behind such a policy. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is to-day following his old tactics; he is hiding behind the officers of his department. Ever since he has had a seat in this House that has been his practice, and he has seemingly not learned anything from the past. Now, the minister should be the defender of his own department. If one of his officers is attacked on the ground of lack of knowledge, lack of discretion or lack of attention, the officer is not to go on a public platform and attack the person criticising in return. It is the minister who is to defend his department and show if he can that he has been well advised and that his officers are doing their duty. I would like to hear from the Prime Minister as to what he thinks of a policy of that kind. We shall have a veritable bear garden if the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is to be in the saddle very long.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I respond with pleasure, and I would say frankly to my hon. friend that I do not believe he has properly apprehended the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. It is true, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries said that Commander Roper was perfectly justified in saying what he did; but what I understood from the minister's remark was that Commander Roper might be excused for saying what he did. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) is quite correct in saying that the minister alone is responsible, and it would be intolerable if any member of the service were to reply on behalf of the government or even on behalf of himself to any criticism of the department or of himself. We have in the service some very estimable gentlemen, and if one of them thinks himself improperly attacked, in parliament or outside, his only recourse is to go to his minister and report that he has been improperly attacked, and ask him to undertake his defence. In this case I have read the remarks of Commander Roper, and I made allowance, as I think everybody would. Being a comparative stranger in the country, and feeling, rightly or wrongly, that he had been attacked, and that his honour was at stake, in a moment which we can forgive, instead of going to his minister, he undertook himself to come before Jhe pub-lie and answer his critics and defend the policy of the department. The only excuse I make for Commander Roper is that he was a perfect stranger. I understand that he is
a most estimable gentleman and I have no doubt he is a gallant officer and most competent in his profession; but, under the circumstances, I think he went out of his way, and while my hon. friend will not say that he was justified, he will at least admit that he might be excused, and by this time no doubt Commander Roper fully appreciates that in this country, as in England, the head of the department alone is responsible for its administration.

I want to be fully understood that I do not wish to be too severe on Commander Roper for this one lapse, and I quite agree with my right hon. friend that, for the reasons he has given, there was some excuse for his conduct; but what I was attacking was the position taken, whether designedly or not, by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur), and that position is not sustained by the Prime Minister.

I would just say a word in this connection. I would first point out that the use of the word ' faction in England, is the same as here, so that it has the same meaning in 'both countries. We know that a very convenient excuse on the part of the minister of Marine and Fisheries, when he has committed himself in any way, is to say that the true interpretation is different from the English; but now we have him resorting to a new excuse, and that is that the meaning in England is not the same as it is in Canada. Well, Mr. Speaker, there is no difference in the meaning in the use of the word * faction ' in tho two countrios. X understood the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur), to say that civil servants were justified in having recourse to the public press or platform .to condemn any member of parliament or ether gentleman who chose to criticise a minister of the Crown or the administration of his department. That certainly was my interpretation of the minister's remarks, and I am very glad to find that the right hon. the Prime Minister had reprimanded him and set him right. But in England, Commander Roper-or whatever may be that officer s rank-would not dare to offer any criticism of any administrative act on tbe part of the British government; and one can only conclude that he must have been put up to do- that in this country by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

My right hon. -friend, who is abundantly endowed with that quality, must have seen that I did not wish to make any regular complaint against Commander Roper, who is a new man and might consequently, have supposed that our civilization is not as advanced as it is. All I wanted was to prevent a recurrence of conduct of this kind; but instead of accepting the suggestion I threw out, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries thought he would do better by referring to newspaper articles which are not pertinent, just as the other day he quoted against my hon. friend from Champlain (Mr. Blondin), citations from newspapers that did not exist.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say that the quotation I have just read is not correct.

Most assuredly it is not. My hon. friend rose to defend himself, and in his defence he read an attack in a newspaper, which he said I had made on Commander Roper, but when called upon to produce that attack, he could not do so. What he read did not justify at all what the minister said. How could I have attacked Commander Roper at the time that article was published when I did not know of his existence, and when he had not even landed in this country? When Commander Roper's speech was published, I telegraphed to Ottawa to know what was his position in the public service. How then could I have intentionally criticised and attacked him as my hon. friend alleges? That .was not possible. But on this occasion, my hon. friend has simply followed the same tactics as on former occasions. When I said that the government officials had refused to furnish the report of the imperial conference of 1909, and laid letters to that effect on the table, my hon. friend the next day read telegrams or letters from the King's Printer in which he said he was forwarding me immediately some 12 or 24 copies of the Marine Bill.

For a copy of the report of the Imperial Defence Committee of the Privy Council in England concerning the defence of the empire, communicated to the Canadian government, and of the despatches and correspondence exchanged between the imperial and the Canadian governments relating to the said report.

He said: The object of this motion is to secure, in order that they may become public property, the plans of defence which' were communicated to all the colonial governments long before the events which led up to the colonial defence conference of 1909. Perhaps the best way in which I can inform the House of the nature of those! documents is to read from a speech made by the Duke of Devonshire on the 3rd of December, 1896, at a meeting of the British Empire League. His Grace said:
I have found with very great satisfaction on my return to office, after an absence from official life of a good many years, the large progress which has been made in the consideration of the great question of imperial defence. A body is now in existence, and has been for many years called the Colonial Defence Committee, composed of representatives of the Admiralty, the War Office and the Colonial Office.
That body has made a complete study of the question of colonial defence as it affects every colony of the British Empire. It has studied the question from the point of view of each colony, and every colony, whether it be a Crown colony or a self-governing colony, is now in possession of the views of Her Majesty's government as to the nature of the attack-the possible attack-to which any of them may be exposed, and as to the means of defence which it is possible to oppose to such attacks. Every colonial government now knows what the imperial government is prepared to undertake in their defence, and what must be left to themselves to undertake. Now, although the instructions to this committee, and the plans which this committee has prepared, are, and must be, to a very great extent, of a confidential character, yet I am permitted to make a public announcement of the principles upon which those plans are based; so that not only the public at home, but every one of our colonial fellow-subjects should know how much it is that the government are prepared to undertake in the defence of the colonies, and the duties which in their turn they think ought to be undertaken by the colonies themselves. These principles are as follows:	The maintenance
of sea supremacy has been assumed as the basis of the system of imperial defence against attacks from over the sea. This is the determining factor in shaping the whole defensive policy of the empire, and is fully recognized by the admiralty, who have accepted the responsibility of protecting all British territory abroad against organized invasion from the sea. To fulfil this great oharge they claim the absolute power of disposing of their forces in the manner they consider most certain to secure success, and object to limit the action of any part of them to the immediate neighbourhood of places which they consider may be more effectively protected by operating at a distance.
It is recognized, however, that Her Majesty's ships engaged in hunting out and destroying the squadrons of the enemy may not be in a position to prevent the predatory raids of hostile cruisers on British ports. The strength of such an attack will vary in the different parts of the world according to the
strength of possibly hostile navies, the proximity of their bases and the troops that are or could easily be brought there in anticipation of war. It also varies from time to time with changing political combination. But it is improbable that this raiding attack would be made by more than a few ships, nor could it be of any permanent effect unless troops could be landed. In no case could a greater force than a few thousand men be collected and conveyed without such arrangements and preparation as would bring the operations under the category of those which the navy has undertaken to prevent.
Against a raid of the nature indicated, it has been considered necessary to make secure those places which are essential to the navy for coaling, refitting, and repairing. Ports for this purpose have been selected by the admiralty, and imperial resources in men and money available for use abroad have been concentrated on their defence. Apart from the harbours fortified for the navy, there are other ports which, though they do not enter into what may be called the general strategic scheme, are also liable from their commercial importance to predatory raids, and which require measures of defence for the protection of the special interests involved. The resources of places which, in the opinion of an enemy, would justify the very considerable risks which a raid on them would involve, are generally sufficient to admit of the provision of local defence by local means; and where the liability to attack and the resources to resist attack co-exist, it has been held to be the duty of the colony to make provision for adequate defence. In dealing with places of this nature the committee have advocated the creation of sufficient fixed defences to prevent their unmolested occupation by hostile cruisers, but more especially the provision of troops sufficient to deal effectively with such forces as an enemy must put on shore to enable him to secure any permanent advantage from his attack. Troops without works may detect an enemy and frustrate his object. Works without troops are useless and delusive. It is necessary to lay stress on this fact-as fortifications give an appearance and feeling of security which is not justified unless they are fully garrisoned by well-trained men and supported by mobile forces, and because expenditure on defences involving a heavy outlay at one time and little at another, can be more easily fitted into the exigencies of fluctuating budgets than expenditure on troops which must be constant to be effective.
I have quoted thus from the speech of the Duke of Devonshire in order to show exactly what was the nature of the defensive measures which, after a long study, this sub-committee of the Imperial Privy Council, or Imperial Cabinet, had seen fit to recommend. It has been adopted by the British government and by that government communicated to all colonial governments to whom that communication could be useful. In confirmation of this, I shall refer to a question which was put by the Earl of Minto in the House of Lords on February 11, 1897, to be found at volume 46 of the Parliamentary Debates in Eng-

land, and the answer to that question of the Earl of Minto by the Duke of Devonshire, in which he reiterates in substance what I have just quoted from his speech to the Imperial Navy League in 1896. After the Duke of Devonshire, then a member of the government, had answered Lord Minto. as reported in the English ' Hansard,' the Earl of Kimberley also joined in-although it was an answer to a question probably he had the right in that House to join in- and confirmed everything that had been stated by the Duke of Devonshire, and added in so many words that that had been for all time up to 1897 the policy of both parties in England as well as apparently the policy of the great dependencies to whom that scheme of defence had been *communicated. It must be apparent to the House that it is very important to us at the present moment, when we are called upon to discuss a different scheme of imperial defence, one which varies considerably from that outlined by the Duke of Devonshire to which I have referred, that which was evolved from the work of the special work of the Privy Council, that we should see that work, be able to refer to it and better understand the one which we have before us in carrying out the present policy.
I also wish to refer the House to the report of the Colonial Conference of 1907, the report which was printed in this country, at page 130 and following, where Lord Tweedmouth, Speaking to the delegates, suggests to them the advisability of cooperating with the British fleet in matters of defence. Lord Tweedmouth propounds no new scheme, he suggests to the colonies no more ample plan of defence, he merely refers to this very plan matured by the Imperial Defence Committee. Lord Tweedmouth, head of the admiralty, on that occasion said: We here at home will undertake to see to the sea supremacy, the supremacy of the admiralty of Great Britain upon the ocean, we will make that our own affair. The protection of the trade routes was also included in the scheme prepared by the committee of the Imperial Privy Council, that was a matter for the mother country. But Lord Tweedmouth insists upon what has been pointed out by the Duke of Devonshire: We want with you ports of refuge, dry docks, important stations for repairing, for coaling; you must undertake in the . dependencies to protect your shores against what the Duke of Devonshire calls any sudden raid or attack, you must be in a position to defend yourselves.
The point which I wish to make in asking for these papers, which I hope the government will see no objection to granting, is to say that in this country at no time has there been any objection to that particular scheme. We have always been ready in Mr. MONK.
the past, we assumed the defence of our own country years ago to the extent of what we could do. If we have spent, during the last 15 years, $60,000,000 and more on our militia and have not a more effective militia, it is surely not the fault of the country, but of those who have had the administration of those funds. In regard to our work upon the waters, my right hon. friend pointed out, at the conference of 1907, that we were policing our own territorial waters and protecting our fisheries, and that possibly we would be obliged to go further in the direction of protecting our coasts. I mean to say that there has never been in this country any objection to the principle of selfdefence. Those who have called us ' Do-nothing men '-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I do not mean that my right hon. friend said that, though there are some of the smaller fry who have spoken of us as do-nothing men. My hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) who sits there smiling, is one of those, and there are others, newcomers. My hon. friend from Nanaimo does not know that for generations we have been ready in Canada to defend our own country, on land, and on sea so far as possible. But the difficulty my right hon. friend has today with regard to his policy-I am speaking of his policy before the election in Drummond and Arthabaska, Ibecause it has been changed a little since then-I am speaking of the policy laid down last session. Now he is gradually veering around to the old policy, which has never been denied in this country, and which was laid down by the Duke of Devonshire. I think I have* sufficiently made known the object we have in view in seeing these communications. We want to understand the history of this matter better than we do now. I do not suppose my right hon. friend is going to object that the scheme is of a confidential nature, because it is not now confidential, whatever it may have been at the origin. If there are parts of it which are not confidential, the Duke of Devonshire referred to that distinction ; we are at all events entitled to know as much as was imparted to the public on the other side, and by eliminating anything of a purely confidential nature we would still be in a position to understand what this plan was.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When I read for the first time the motion of my hon. friend as appearing in the ' Votes and Proceedings,' I did not quite understand what he was aiming at. The words ' plans of defence '. suggest a delicate matter. My hon. friend knows that there are plans of defence which could not be communicated to parliament under any circumstances.

But now that I have heard him explain that what he wants is not a technical plan of defence-as to the existence of which I have no knowledge at all-'but what he wants, I understand, is information concerning a general contribution by the new dominions to the defence of the empire, which has been outlined and discussed at different times for the last Sixteen years. To this there is no objection whatever. Everything which is not of a secret nature and that can be brought down, will be gladly produced, because I am sure-I will not say I am sure, but I will say that when it is produced it ought to dispel many of the illusions under which my hoh. friend has been labouring for the last six or seven months, and which he has been endeavouring to communicate to the people of Quebec, particularly of those of Drum-mond-Arthabaska. He will find that there is no foundation for his suspicion that Canada is being drawn into the military armaments of England. Let me say in conclusion that I was highly pleased at the declaration which I now hear from my hon. friend, that his party has been ready at all times to contribute to the defence of the country-at all times except the present time.
Motion agreed to.

upon which they claim the right of recognition bears upon the question: Are their duties of a diplomatic character, or solely of a commercial character? For instance, at the present time, Mr. Foster, the able and distinguished consul-general of the United States at Ottawa, is one of the commissioners duly accredited by his country to negotiate a reciprocity treaty with Canada. A few months ago the negotiations for a better trade understanding between Germany and Canada were conducted on the part of Germany by the consul general of that country, Dr. Long, of Montreal.

There is also another phase of this question to which I desire to draw attention. In the Table of Precedence set forth in the parliamentary guide there are 33 distinctively defined positions, commencing with the Governor General and coming down to retired fudges. It will be observed that in this list no reference whatever is made to the clergy of any denomination except-
Archbishops and bishops by seniority.
Why, in a country which has no state church, recognition is accorded to any one or two denominations and not to others is a mystery to me. It is bound to cause friction or unpleasantness among the churches.
But, apart from this single mention of the churches, some individual has set himself up as an authority and has added to the Table of Precedence. for an answer from the right hon. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can, to a large extent, sympathize with the views which have been expressed by my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule), and I may say that, in my humble judgment, the question is much iarger even than he has represented it. The Table of Precedence is now as old as confederation; I think it was promulgated in 1867, or 1868. It is full of inconsistencies and incongruities, and ought to be reformed at an early date. Indeed, His Excellency the Governor General has himself reformed it in many particulars. In regard, for instance, to the position assigned to the churches, only two churches are recognized in the Table of Precedence- the English church and the Roman Catholig church. All other denominations had been ignored. I may say at once to my hon. friend that in so far as he finds fault with the invitation extended to the Vicar general of the diocese of Ottawa, I do not think his objection holds good, because the Vicar general of the diocese was the administrator of the diocese, and it was in that capacity, in the absence of the bishop, that he was invited to the last drawing room.
In other words he was bishop for the time being.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He was representing the bishop for the time being. In regard to the statement of my hon. friend as to Dr. Herridge, and Dr. Cameron-both eminent divines of this city and both gentlemen who are a credit to the community- not being invited I think the hon. gentleman is in error. Perhaps Dr. Herridge or Dr. Cameron were not invited themselves, but, although I have no information on the point I think that the heads of the Presbyterian church, the Methodist church, and the Baptist church were invited this year as for some years past. I do not know who is at present the moderator of the Presbyterian General Assembly, but whoever he be I am quite sure he received an invitation. I am sure also that the head of the Methodist body-if the Methodist body can be said to have a head-was also invited, and in the same way the representative of the Baptist church. I may say that His Ex-

eeiiency the Governor General, ignoring in this respect the Table of Precedence, and giving heed to what is undoubtedly the spirit of the Canadian people, has of late years taken upon himself to invite to his table on state occasions representatives of the different religious denominations in this country. I hope that will be satisfactory to my hon. friend. I must disclaim, however, any responsibility in this connection. It is not part of the advice which I have to give to His Excellency the Governor General. The Governor General has acted upon his own initiative and I know that in this, as in other instances he has corrected the Table of Precedence so as to make it more acceptable and more up to date than it was some years ago.
The motion of my hon. friend has special reference to the consuls general, and it reads:
For a copy of any memorials, correspondence, &c., between His Excellency the Governor General and the Colonial Office, or between any member of the government, and the Foreign Consuls General in Canada, relative to the status of the latter, at official functions, such as the Vice-regal Drawing Room.
The consuls general of the different countries residing in Ottawa, perform important duties. Their status at the present time, in view of our development as a nation-as I have sometimes stated-is at present undetermined and undefined. If the consuls general were in England, or in any country which has absolute independence they *would have no status whatever such as is contemplated in this motion. However, the consuls general perform with us very important duties; duties not only of a commercial nature, but even of a semi-diplomatic nature. Indeed, the development of Canada to its present status can hardly bo defined. I have often taken the view that vve ere now a nation, and in fact in many respects we have the power and the duty and responsibility of a nation. But, we cannot have under present conditions diplomatic agents amongst us other than the consular- agents who are entrusted by their governments with commercial functions. But, by the force of things these consuls general have become with us semi-diplomatic agents, and many of the consuls have realiy performed in Canada diplomatic duties. The American consul, Mr. Foster, has been acting for his government in what is a diplomatic function, and the consul of Italy and the consul of Germany were charged with similar duties last year. Ail this has been done without authority, and is contrary to the rules that apply among civilized nations, but it became a necessity because of the development of the larger colonies of the British Empire which have become practically nations. Now, I believe we should endeavour to determine by
law, or rather somewhat officially, what the rights and status, of the consuls general of the different nations are. Practically they are diplomatic agents as well as consular agents, and for my part I think it would be proper that at an early date their official position should be defined. I think we should have an understanding with the 'm-perial government that the consuls should be allowed semi-diplomatic recognition amongst us. This is a matter which I suppose concerns Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa as well as Canada, and probably it may be a proper subject for discussion at the next imperial conference. If there are any papers such as are called for bv the motion, they will be brought down
