The prerogative of His Majesty is carefully guarded in that respect, and the only possible way in which we can make any change in the Table of Precedence is to make suggestions to the imperial authorities which suggestions may or may not be acted upon. We have to follow the order of precedence which is communicated to us.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.
As a burning and shining light, in one of the large democratic churches

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman speaking of himself?

Yes. As one who believes in the old principle of co-operative democracy rather than the principle of autocracy, I may be permitted to correct the first minister. The Methodist church has a president; in fact they have a general superintendent and an assistant superintendent for the whole of Canada. They have a president of each conference, and a chairman of every district, which is a much more important office than the Vicar-general would hold in the city of Ottawa, as the chairman of the Ottawa district is also administrator for the church in this locality.
Some years ago, when this matter came up, the late Hon. Sir John Thompson took the view which the right hon. the First Minister does, that in this Table of Precedence the heads of all the churches should be recognized officially.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That has been carried out.

Sir John Thompson's view was that the senior officer should take precedence, so that the moderator of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church on one occasion took precedence over archbishops and bishops of the Anglican and Roman Catholic churches. These are trifling matters, but they are annoying. If we are going to have this semi-officiai union of church and state in Canada, a thing which I have no use for whatever, it should be carried out in a spirit of fair play to all.

It is satisfactory to have the intimation of the right hon. the First Minister that it is intended to have this Table of Precedence revised at an early date and to do what many think is only simple justice to the consuls general in Canada. It seems to me that the greatness of the countries which these gentlemen represent demands consideration. To place men occupying these distinguished positions below the mayor of a city or the Mr. J. HAGGART.
sheriff of a county is hardly respectful to the countries they represent. The right hon. the First Minister, if I understood him correctly, intimated that he had nothing to do with this list. We hold the government responsible generally for everything ; and when we are in doubt, we hold the premier responsible, because we take for granted that he is the person above all others charged with seeing that everything is done rightly. If I understood him correctly, he said that we . did not interfere with the order of precedence as laid down by the Colonial Office. But this very list does interfere with it. Where that was made up I do not know. I am credibly informed that it was not made up by the Governor General. It was probably made up by some subordinate, and in that- list are included names not furnished by the Colonial Office at all. In the Colonial Office list there is nothing about the Vicar-general. The only reference to churches is where it speaks of archbishops and bishops according to seniority. Yet in this list published in the ' Evening Journal ' the Vicar-general is included, while there is nothing about bishops or archbishops at all. So that it is clear that an amendment has been made in the list by some person. Whether it has been done unwittingly or otherwise, it has been done improperly. There ought to be sufficient supervision over it by some one to insure that no injustice is done to any and that fair play is done to all.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. LANCASTER moved second reading of Bill (No. 2), to amend the Railway Act. He said : Mr. Speaker, the legislation that I am proposing has long been wanted in the country, and I understood from time to time that the government was going to introduce something of the kind. But as that has not been done, I have thought it my duty to bring it forward. It has to do with the lives of the people, so many of which are destroyed by the railways of the country. The number of deaths caused by the railways throughout Canada is still appalling, notwithstanding the efforts that have been made from time to time to diminish them. It is thought by many people who have spoken to me on the subject, and I am of the same opinion, that if there were investigations by coroners into all these fatalities, the number of deaths would probably be decreased, because if a servant of a railway were found guilty of negligence, he would be liable to be charged with manslaughter, and, knowing this, he would of necessity be more careful.

If on the other hand the victim is found to have been killed through his own carelessness, the public mind would be satisfied and be under no misapprehension about the facts. If anybody be found dead on private property, a coroner's inquest is always held. I am sorry to say, however, that many coroners are also physicians for railway companies, and if the coroner comes to the conclusion, from information he receives, and which is not under oath and which no one else hears, that an inquest is not necessary, he decides not to hold any. I do not wish to be understood as saying that the majority of coroners, when they decide not to hold an inquest, are not really convinced that an inquest is not necessary, but the fact remains that the evidence on which a coroner comes to such a decision is not given under oath and is given behind the backs of people quietly and secretly, and the information which might be forthcoming if an inquest were held, might be of such a nature that it would change the coroner's opinion. Neither do I wish to be understood as saying that the majority of coroners are in the employ of railway companies, but a good many are and no harm would be done-and great good may possibly be done -if legislation such as I propose be enacted. It might be well if I were to read the Bill:
Section 292 of the Railway Act, chapter 37 of the revised statutes 1906, is amended by adding the following subsection:
Whenever any person is killed, or receives injuries causing death, on the property of, or by or in a train of, any company, the coroner of the county in which such death or injuries occur, and resident nearest to the place at which such death or injuries occurred, shall hold an inquest on the body of the person so killed immediately upon receiving notice of such death.
Section 292 provides that where accidents occur the Railway Commission shall get a report from the railway company and provides further that the board may declare, by regulation, the manner and form in which such notice and report shall be given by the railway company.
Having had a great deal to do with the Railway Act since it was passed, I might here point out that it would be well if the whole Act were codified so that the subjects connected with each other might be grouped together in one part of the Act. At present you have to look through half a dozen portions of the law to find out all the provisions on any particular branch of the subject. Let me give an illustration. A year or so ago I had to argue before the Supreme Court that the Railway Commission had power to order stations to be established at the time of beginning the works by railway companies already running trains and operating them; and we had to discuss some 25 or 30 sections in different parts of the Railway. Act, out of some 400
sections, in order to arrive at a conclusion. There are, however, a couple of sections which are headed accidents, and that is where I thought it most likely people would look for the legislation I now suggest and that is where I ask to have it inserted. I would simply point out that in cases of fatal accidents, there could be no harm in having a public inquest held so that the jury might find out what caused the death Where a railway is not concerned, the result sometimes is an arrest for manslaughter because of the verdict of the coroner's jury, but we need not trouble ourselves about the effect of the verdict, because that verdict cannot be used in the prosecution or defence. It shows, however, that a coroner's inquest was held and thus allays the public mind.
There can be no serious results to anybody, as the verdict of a coroner's jury has no legal effect as tending to convict or excuse anybody, or in a civil action; but at such an inquest the facts can be made known, those who are acquainted with them can tell them publicly and we will not have the present condition in which it is possible for some one to see the coroner and load him up privately with a statement of the circumstances not given under oath. As a rule when there is a death from accident an inquest is held, and I do not suggest that generally in railway cases inquests are not held, but I have had complaints in my office of three deaths on railways in one year in the neighbourhood of St. Catharines where no inquests were held. The public are much dissatisfied. A coroner was notified in each case but in each case he said he had inquired from the railway officials and was satisfied that the persons were killed in a certain way and therefore he did not think an inquest necessary. That does not satisfy the public, publicity is what they want and that is denied them. The railway people, for their own salvation, should be anxious to have these inquests. If, at an inquest it is shown that the victim met his death through his own carelessness the verdict serves as a warning to other people, and children are warned by their parents and friends and the effect of the verdict pointed out to them. On the other hand, if it is shown that the railway is to blame, that thei switchman was not attending to his duty, that he was drunk or asleep at the switch,'' he is put on trial for manslaughter and because of the evidence obtained at the* coroner's inquest, he may or may not be convicted; but the public will be satisfied that something is being done in the direev tion of protecting them. Publicity is the great salvation and the great educator. No matter what the result of the investigation may be, full publicity, in my

humble opinion, is what will benefit both sides and have a tendency to prevent these' fatalities. The public are not satisfied to have matters go on as they are. Deaths occur which are not investigated, and I thought it my duty to introduce this Bill because I think it would be wise legisla-i tion and, as I have said, it cannot hurt anybody.

'GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).- The object of this Bill is good, I have no objection to the ob7 ject which my hon. friend has in view. There has, however, been complaint in some parts of Ontario that coroners were too apt to hold investigations and people! have complained of. the expense of hold4 ing investigations in some cases where, there was really no reasonable doubt as to the cause of death. However, that would not apply in the case of railway accidents, I admit that. I agree with my hon. friend as to the codifying of the Railway Act but conditions are changing so rapidly, particularly in the west, that I have not rushed to suggest it, because I think quite a number of amendments to the Act will still be required to meet all the conditions. I agree that the Act is growing to such proportions that it is bet coming cumbersome, and even those who make the Act and try to administer it from day to day sometimes find difficulty1 in putting their hand on that part of the Act under which they wish to proceed. Coroners are the appointees of the provincial governments, not our appointees Could we pass an Act to compel the employees of some other government to work for us? The coroners' duties, the coroJ ners' reports and investigations, are all under provincial authority.
You order an inquiry in the case of an accident on a ship.
As I understand the provincial statutes govern the duties of the coroners, and if we pass a statute it might conflict with the duties imposed on them by their employers, the provincial authorities.

Does my hon. friend think it could possibly conflict in a matter that is entirely under the jurisdiction of the Dominion government, the control of Dominion railways? The trouble is that the provincial legislature' cannot legislate on anything that affects a railway.

Not that affects a railway, but they can pass an Act dealing with an accident caused by a railway, and do so every day. Their coroners hold inauests every day by order of the attorney general, and I hesitate to pass an Act taking the coroners in any way under our jurisdiction, Mr. LANCASTER.
when, as a matter of fact, they are entirely and solely under provincial jurisdiction.
Is there no way in which we could get at this trouble without interfering with the provincial authorities? I am in sympathy with the object of my hon. friend, but I would suggest that if he would call the attention of the provincial authorities to what he thinks is a deficiency in their law, and ask them to make it compulsory to hold inquests into deaths caused by railway accidents, that would simplify the whole matter. Or we can pass an Act not to interfere with the coroners, but to compel the railway to notify the coroner of every accident, as we now compel them to notify the Board of Railway Commissioners; or we could order and compel them to notify the attorney general of the province in which an accident occurs, and the attorney general could instruct his officers to hold an inquest. I have here -chapter 97 of the Revised Statutes of Ontario, an Act respecting coroners, so you see the coroners are their officials, not ours. Section 2 says:-
2.	Except as provided in the next two sections, no inquest shall be held on the body of any deceased person by a coroner until it has been made to appear to him that there is reason to believe that the deceased died from violence or unfair means, or by culpable or negligent conduct of others, under such circumstances as require investigation, and not through mere accident or mischance.
You see the Ontario Statute really limits them, tells them they must not rush to hold inquests unless they have reason to believe inquests are necessary.
Section 3 provides further:

3.	Upon the death of a prisoner, the warden, jailer, keeper or superintendent of the penitentiary, jail, prison, house of correction, lock-up house, or house of industry in which the prisoner dies, shall immediately give notice thereof to some coroner of the county, city or town in which the death has taken place, and the coroner shall proceed forthwith to hold an inquest upon the body except in the case of a death taking place in any county house of industry in which case such inquest shall not be necessary, unless after notification, the County Crown Attorney believes that such death took place under circumstances requiring investigation.
Now, if the provincial authority would put another clause in there saying that the coroner should proceed to hold an investigation wherever death is caused by an accident on a railway, the whole case would be covered without our interference.
We have said that as to the provincial authorities.

They legislate as to the coroner's duties, not as to the railways, and whenever a man may be found dead.

the matter comes under the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities and the consideration of the coroner.
The question that arises is whether the provincial authority has the power of making any such regulations. Is it vested in them or in the Dominion?

I think it is vested in the provincial authorities, without doubt, and in them alone. Now, let me tell my hon. friend why I think so. Very frequently inquests are held on the bodies of victims of railway accidents, and no one ever stops to ask whether the coroner is a Dominion or a provincial officer. In the town of Brockville accidents frequently occur, and the coroner at once holds an inquest, and the question has never been raised. It is not the railway that he is investigating, but it is the death of the victim, and the provincial authorities have a right to have their coroner hold that inquest, and they are the only authority that can command the coroner to do anything because he is their appointee. Now, here is section 7 of the Ontario Act :
It shall not be lawful for a coroner to conduct an inquest in any case where loss of life has been caused at or on a railroad, mine or other work whereof he is owner or part owner, either as a shareholder or otherwise, nor_ in any like case at or on a work where he is employed as medical attendant by the owner thereof, or by any agreement or understanding direct or indirect with the employees at or on such work.
It points out that no coroner can hold an inquest on a death that occurs on a railway in which he is personally interested, either on behalf of the men or on behalf of the railway.
But the coroner may say that an inquest is not necessary, and having said so, none is held.

I am not disagreeing with my hon. friend, I am pointing out that it is the provincial authority which controls the coroner. I would join my hon. friend in calling this to the attention of the provincial authorities throughout the Dominion, and asking them whether it would not be wise to make such a provision.
Would it not be well that when a death occurs on a railway the railway company should notify the county attorney, and leave the rest to the provincial law?

I would be content to do that. I want to meet the view of my hon. friend, if he would make his Bill so that the railway company must notify the county attorney, or the coroner, or the Attorney General of the province. I 31
think, perhaps, to notify the county attorney would be the quickest way to get at it, except in some districts where there are none. In that case they might notify the Attorney General. I feel like compelling the railways to call the attention of the proper authorities to the fact that a death has occurred, and it is their duty to order an inquest. We cannot order a coroner to do anything as he is not under our authority.

I think you could notify the coroner. One of the duties of a coroner, when he is notified that a death has taken place, is to look into the circumstances and decide for himself whether an inquest is necessary.

The objection to that would be that the railway company would be suspected of selecting a coroner friendly to themselves ; whereas if they notified the county attorney, or any official of that character, there would be no suspicion of the kind, because the county attorney would see to the selection of the coroner.

I would say, take the
nearest coroner. The objection I see to notifying the county attorney is, that great delays might occur, where you might have to notify a man living thirty or forty miles away from the scene of the accident. Perhaps no one knows where the nearest coroner lives, and as the body cannot be removed until a coroner reaches the place, delay and trouble would occur.

I am inclined to agree with my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr Barker), particularly in face of the Ontario statute, which says that any coroner who is a medical adviser of the men, or a medical attendant, or has any connection with the railway, cannot act. The nearest coroner might be one who could not hold an inquest, and then possibly he would report that none was necessary.
No, my Bill says that he should hold one.

I think the safest way, would be to notify the county attorney, where there is one, and where there is not one, then the Attorney General of the province. That can be done by wire. I want to meet the views of my hon. friend in his object, but I think we would not have a right to pass legislation which would interfere with the provincial Act, or assume jurisdiction where we have none.

The question is one of jurisdiction. When a coroner is holding an inquest he is acting as judge in a criminal case, and the rules and procedures in criminal cases are under the jurisdiction of the Dominion government. Then the question arises whether the juris-



diction is in this House or the provincial House. I am not clear upon the subject, and I want information. Since the judge is acting as in a criminal case, the rules and procedures of which are prescribed by the Dominion government, the question arises whether an inquest comes under that category or not, and whether the rules and procedures should be made by the Dominion or the provincial authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can scarcely agree with my hon. friend that the coroner is acting in a judicial capacity, though the result of his labours may have an important bearing upon a subsequent criminal charge. But it is clear that the duties of a coroner are those entirely of an investigating character. Nobody is upon trial before a coroner's jury. Frequently the result of the coroner's inquest is a verdict showing that the jury has not been able to come to a conclusion as to who the person may be, who is responsible for the matteT they are investigating. The office of coroner is a very ancient one, and the duties of a coroner are well enough defined by the courts in their decisions through the centuries during which that office has been known to English law. But under our Canadian system, nothing, I think, can be more clear than that the whole power of legislating in regard to the office and the duty of a coroner rests with the provincial authorities. They have exercised that power in some instances, possibly not in all the provinces-as to that, I am not aware. But in the province of Ontario the statute lays down many restrictions upon the action of coroners. Now it would conflict at once with some of those provisions if this parliament were to enact that in every case of death, occurring upon a rail- way, and by the way, this Bill, apparently, would extend even to a death resulting from natural causes, 'but certainly in every case in which death resulted by reason of an accident from a railway, there must be an inquest. The Ontario statute provides that it is only in certain circumstances that there is to be an inquest, and ought m,(, to court a conflict between an Enactment of this parliament and the provincial legislation? There are statutes on the subject in other provinces with the various provisions of which we are not familiar. We should very probably be running counter to some of those provisions if we were to enact this Bill in the shape in which it is presented and in these circumstances it certainly would seem an injudicious thing, and I would, with all deference, submit we should not pass such legislation, the necessity for which, I would respectfully submit, does not very clearly appear.
I am sure that hon. gentlemen in the House will agree with me in the knowledge, as a matter of personal experience, that in Mr. HAGGART.
the province of Ontario, at any rate, coroners' inquests in case of death resulting from an accident upon a railway are very frequent. I have a very vivid recollection of a railway accident some years ago in which I happened to have been, and in regard to which I appeared as a witness on the coroners' inquest on the occasion of the death of other passengers. As a matter of ordinary legal practice I know that it is-not, of course, an occurrence of every day, but a most frequent occurrence for inquests to be held in respect of accidents upon every railway, whether a Dominion railway or a provincial railway. I have never heard that there was any lack of these inquests, and I think that the statute of Ontario makes provision rather in the way of preventing inquests except where they are necessary. It seems to me that this would be legislation in the other direction. I think the evil which led to the passing of the Ontario statute was that frequently where death occurred there was a competition among foreigners for the fees-which resulted from the holding of the inquest and because that was not a seemly thing and because it was thought there ought to be some restriction shown about the holding of these inquests and that they should not be held as a matter of course, the Ontario legislation was passed providing that it was only in certain circumstances that they should be permitted.
I suppose the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) will admit that the only power of appointing coroners rests with the provincial governments?
No, I do not admit that. I say it has been done, but I also say that we can appoint them if we want to.
Any way the hon. gentleman admits that up to tne present time the government of Canada has never appointed coroners?
That may be.
Suppose the nearest coroner were a provincial coroner and we order him to hold an inquest and he refuses; what will happen?

Then, the next nearest one will hold it. I assume that if the nearest coroner refuses to all intents and purposes he is dead under the Act and that after him the next nearest one will act and he will be the next nearest under the circumstances. I do not think we need be afraid of a situation of that kind. It is manifest that the House is with me in thinking that this legislation is necessary. It is quite evident even from what the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) says and from the more frank statement of the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) that legislation of this kind is necessary.

There is no reason to be afraid about jurisdiction. When was this government ever afraid about jurisdiction when they wanted to remedy-an evil or accomplish something which they said was for the welfare of this country? What did the leader-I will not say of the government-but of some of the members of this government-the much respected and well known Sir Oliver Mowat, say on one occasion? If there is any question about jurisdiction I am going to assume that we have jurisdiction and I am going to let the courts decide that we have not if they dare. We can appoint coroners if we want to. I am not suggesting that we should, but I am not troubled a bit by all this technicality about a coroner being appointed by the provincial government in a Dominion railway matter. I am not suggesting that we should have two sets of coroners! But, what about magistrates and justices of the peace? We do not appoint the magistrates and the justices of the peace, but they have to take the Criminal Code and, under hundreds of sections, they have to carry out the bequests of this parliament. Yet, every one is appointed by the provincial government. Jurisdiction! Why jurisdiction exists to carry out, under the decision of the Privy Council in several well known cases, anything that is necessary in order to carry out a subject matter that is within the jurisdiction of the Dominion parliament. We have jurisdiction over Dominion railways. We have the right then to exercise any jurisdiction supplementary to that, in assistance or furtherance of it, in order to carry out such an undertaking, just the same as we have the right to say that they shall cross the highways of a province with a Dominion railway. Why can this parliament allow a Dominion railway to cross provincial highways without the consent of the provincial government in whom, under the British North America Act, all the powers are vested with regard to these highways? Simply because it is necessary to cross these highways in order to carry out the object of the legislation, the creation of a Dominion railway. That principle has been decided over and over again and the Minister of Justice surely knows it. If the Minister of Justice is of the same mind as the Minister of Railways and wants to prevent what is admitted on both sides of the House to be an evil in the country, whv cannot he assume that we have jurisdiction and say to the coroner in the country :	In regard to a Dominion matter you
shall do so and so while you are a coroner. We do not appoint the coroner any more than we appoint the magistrate or the justice of the peace or several other officials who exist simply by the authority of the provincial legislature, but the magistrates and justices of the peace put in force the provisions of the Criminal Code, which is 314
Dominion legislation just the same as the Railway Act is Dominion legislation in so-far as Dominion railways are concerned and, of course, the legislation of this parliament only applies to Dominion railways.
I did not hear the observations of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth), but was it not laid down by the Minister of Justice six or seven years ago in connection with the-Election Act-
The Manitoba elections.

No, but the General Franchise Act, that it was proper for this parliament to impose duties upon a provincial officer and that it could properly do so with respect to matters over which the parliament of Canada had jurisdiction?
Yes.

That matter was very seriously debated at the time, -a great many arguments pro and con were-advanced in this House, and the final conclusion, as voiced by the Minister of Justice, was that such jurisdiction undoubtedly did exist in this parliament.

There is no doubt of that, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Justice laid it down, as stated by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), that we had such jurisdiction, and in so doing he only did what all who are lawyers in this House, at all events, and I think most of the laymen, quite understand. It is a well known principle laid down by the Privy Council in several cases that we have the right to interfere, if you like, to use a strong expression, with provincial matters in so far as that interference is necessary in order to properly carry out legislation in regard to a subject matter over which we have control. That is exactly why we can allow a Dominion railway to go over a provincial highway without the consent of the provincial authorities. If we enact that a railway shall run from Toronto to Winnipeg, say, it must cross highways, and if the provincial government can prevent it doing so without legislation the result must be to render nugatory the Tights of the Dominion parliament.
We, therefore, have ordered the magistrates to do a number of things, and the magistrates are appointed by the provincial government. In view of the argument of the Minister of Justice, he will be surprised to learn that in the Criminal Code itself he tells coroners what they must do, and that being so, why cannot he tell them what they must do in the Dominion Railway Act? Section 667 of the Criminal Code says that these coroners, whom the Minister of Jus-

tice is afraid to overwork, must do certain things. It reads:-
Every coroner, upon any inquisition taken before him whereby any person is charged with manslaughter or murder, shall, if the person or persons, or either of them, affected by the (verdict or finding (is mot already charged with the said offence before a magistrate or justice, by warrant under his hand, direct that such person be taken into custody and be conveyed, with all convenient speed, before a magistrate or justice; or such coroner may direct such person to enter into a recognizance before him, with or without a surety or sureties, to appear before a magistrate or justice.
2. In either case, it shall be the duty of the coroner to transmit to such magistrate or justice the deposition taken before him iu the matter.
Here we have it set out In the Criminal Code what the duty of coroners shall be, and in that section coroners and magistrates are coupled together, and this Dominion parliament tells them what are their duties. I thought., in my simplicity, that when, in my Bill, I used the_ same words as are to be found in the Criminal Code, that the legislation I propose might be found to be consistent with Dominion legislation. But the Minister of Justice seems to take a different view, although I do not think any one who considers the matter will dare to say that we have no power to order an official of the provincial government to carry out the objects of Dominion legislation. I am sorry that this purely technical and unmeritorious objection is raised by the Minister of Justice, and if it is going to be insisted upon I shall have the termerity to divide the House on the question. I am not wedded to the language set out in my Bill; it- may be that the object I seek may be attained by other wording, but before I desist from pressing the measure I will have to hear some better reasons than those advanced by the Minister of Justice.

If my hon. friend will allow the Bill to stand we will confer about it and perhaps we can come to some agreement which will prevent our usurping the powers, as I think, of the provincial parliaments. I am in sympathy with the object my hon. friend has in view, but I do not think he should undertake to deal with the coroners.
I have no objection to that so long as I have assurance that the Bill will retain its place on the Orderi Paper, or that it will be submitted as a government motion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will keep its place on the Order Paper, and I move the adjournment of the debate.
I will not object to that so long as it is agreed that we shall have an opportunity to discuss the matter again.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will remain on the top of the list.
Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.

Mr. MILLER moved second reading of Bill (No. 6) to amend the Interest Act. He said: This Bill is almost exactly similar to the Bill I introduced last year and which passed its second reading and the committee stage, and stood for third reading, but was not reached. It permits the mortgagor to pay off an overdue mortgage by giving one month's notice of his intention to do so, or by paying one month's extra interest by way of bonus. It applies only to an overdue mortgage; it is not retroactive, but only refers to mortgages made or renewed after this date. The Bill met with the favour of the House last session. It seems to me that a man should have the same right to pay off an overdue mortgage that he has to pay off an overdue note. Last session Mr. Osier, one of the members for Toronto, who has a good deal to do with financial and monev lending companies, stated that he could see no wrong in the Bill, and other leading financial men in Toronto have spoken to me in a similar manner. Last session the Minister of Public Works thought that perhaps the Bill might imply that no mortgagor, no matter what was or was not in his contract, could pay off an overdue mortgage unless by giving notice or paying the bonus referred to in this Act. Subsection 2 of the Bill removes that difficulty. Mr. Osier, among others, thought that the mortgagor ought not to be able to give notice repeatedly and, failing to carry out his expressed intention cause annoyance to the mortgagee. Subsection 3 provides that if the mortgagor gives notice and does not avail himself of it, that he should have no further privilege in that regard.
I would like to see that Bill go further than it does, and I would like to know what the hon. member (Mr. Miller) means exactly by paying off an overdue mortgage.

Mortgages are usually made for a term of five years and when the mortgagor has had the money for five years the term of the mortgage expires, and no matter what provision may be in his mortgage that may bind him to give three months' notice or pay three months' interest before he has the privilege of paying off the mortgage, the mortgage having expired he will have the right to pay off this mortgage

by giving one month's notice of his intention' or paying one month's interest in lieu of notice.
As a matter of fact, almost all mortgages are drawn so that they may be paid off when they become due.
Oh, yes, but not afterwards unless by notice or bonus.

I think most of the mortgages in our country are drawn in that way. What I would like to see is permission under certain conditions to pay a mortgage before it becomes due. By way "of illustration, I will state what occurred in my own case last year. I bought some land on which a mortgage had been put the year before by the previous owner at a very high rate of interest, 8 per cent. When I bought the land I did not wish to pay 8 per cent interest. I wanted to pay off the mortgage, so that) I might, if I wished, put on another at a lower rate of interest ; but I was unable to do so. The consequence is that I have to continue paying 8 per cent on that mortgage for 5 years.
I would advise my hon. friend not to buy the land under those circumstances.

The hon. gentleman does not quite understand the situation. The mortgage was not equal to the value of the land, and I may have made a very profitable investment even with that mortgage on it. If such a provision as I suggest is not put into this Bill, I intend to bring a Bill into the House to admit of mortgages under certain conditions being paid off before they become due.

Loan companies, life insurance companies and other companies lending money on land mortgages have done and are doing a great deal to assist in opening up the western country, and it would be grossly unfair to them to enact the provision which the hon. member suggests, for this reason. Suppose the prevailing rate of interest in the west to-day is 7 per cent, and a man borrows money at that rate on a five years' mortgage. That is the best bargain he can make at the time. If money goes up to 8 per cent, the lender cannot, under any provision of the mortgage, demand from the borrower an additional one per cent ; but if the prevailing rate of interest fell to 6 per cent during the currency of the mortgage, the consequence of such a law as my hon. friend suggests would be that every borrower would pay off his mortgage, and the mortgagees would have their vaults full of money, with no opportunity to lend it. The privilege would be altogether onesided.

My hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) has not evidently taken sufficient time to consider the prope sition he has made, because a contract is purely a provincial matter entirely under the jurisdiction of provincial laws. If A agrees to pay B 8 per cent interest for four or five years, that is a contract, oyer which this parliament has no jurisdiction what ever. My hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) is attempting to obtain his object by providing that after a certain notice is given, no further interest shall be chargeable. We cannot compel the mortgagee to take his money, but we can say that after a certain time he cannot charge more interest, because under the British North America Act this parliament has jurisdiction over interest.
Is not that merely over the rate of interest? Have we any right to make any stipulation as to the contract surrounding it?

My hon. friend has asked me a question which it might be somewhat difficult to answer, I think, however, that if we have jurisdiction to legislate regarding interest, we have jurisdiction to legislate on anything respecting interest. However, that is a matter which perhaps does not arise just now. I can only say to my hon. friend from Manitoba that if he only wishes to attain the object he has in view, the legislature of the province of Manitoba has" absolute jurisdiction to pass such legislation, and that is the source to which he should apply 'or it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not intend to offer any violent opposition to the passing of this Bill, but I will say at once that I do not like it. I think it is interfering with the freedom of contract which might much better be left alone. I certainly believe in free trade, and equally I believe in the unhampered right of any person of full age and of sound sense to make his own bargains, and I thins mat any effort which a legislature makes to protect a man against himself is simply going to recoil upon the head of the very individual whom the legislature is trying to save. Now, what is going to be the effect of this legislation? Surely it is perfectly plain that if this Bill becomes law, every mortgagee will see that his money is paid when it is due or that he has a new agreement that will postpone the due day. A moneylender with his eyes_ open, who knows what the law is, is going to see to it that he does not subject himself to what is, practically a penalty, namely, the loss of his interest, if this Bill is to operate upon his particular transaction, and if you drive the money-lender to do that, you damage the very borrower to protect whom is the principal object of this Bill.
How would you damage 'the mortgagor in that case? '

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You damage the mortgagor by making the mortgagee harder upon him. The lender, if he knows that his interest is to continue running after the date for payment, will probably be perfectly content to leave things as they are, and not press the borrower, who has been unable to pay on the due date. But if the Bill should become law, the lender will know that, on notice being given him, lie is liable to be paid off summarily or to [DOT] lose the subsequent interest, and he will take care that he does not allow the date of payment to pass without exacting it or getting a new agreement postponing payment another twelve months or two years. So that you are going to force the lender to be less lenient than he would be if you liad not passed the legislation. I quite admit that the same remark applies to the legislation we have already and to which the Bill proposes an amendment. I am mot questioning our power to pass it. It "was thought by the wise men of some 20 [DOT]or 25 years ago, who passed the former Act, that we had power to legislate in that way notwithstanding that legislation interfered with the right of contract, and I am not going to discuss that question; but [DOT]granted that we have the power, I am strongly of the opinion that there is no necessity to exercise it, and that it would be injudicious to do so in the interests of the borrower himself. Surely in this day and generation every one knows that the -average borrower is on perfect equality with the average lender. The two are free alike to make their own contract, and there is just as much competition in the lending as in the borrowing. There is therefore no difficulty in the borrower getting a perfectly straighforward and plain ^contract to prove the relations with the lender. In those circumstances, to seek to impose a different contract upon him or to put the lender in any position which will force him to take some means; whereby he can secure himself at the expense of the borrower, would not, I think, he in the interests of the borrower himself.

I would like, to ask the mover of the Bill whether or not he has made any inquiry as to the laws prevailing in the different provinces with respect to mortgage contracts? This is legislation, not designed for one province but which will affect nine provinces, and I am not sure that it would be perfectly acceptable in all the provinces, having, regard to the laws and customs of each.

I would like to understand the meaning of the expression contained in the first three lines.
' Any principal money, interest or other money.' Well, that other money perhaps might be an insurance premium, or it might be taxes.

What is the meaning of the expression that immediate-

ly follows: ' By mortgage made, or renewed by renewal or extension agreement '?

Suppose a mortgage be made to mature on the 1st of January, 1911, then this Act does not apply. Should there be a new mortgage made on the maturity of that mortgage, that would bring it within the Act. In practice these mortgages are frequently renewed by giving a new mortgage, or by a renewal or extension agreement, which is not registered in the registry office, although each party may have a copy. Now by the renewal of that mortgage by extension agreement, I mean to bring it under the same stipulations as if a new mortgage had been taken.
I think the hon. member is frustrating the object he has in view. ' Made or renewed by renewal or extension agreement.' Suppose it is made by a new mortgage, that is a renewal.
If it is renewed by a new mortgage after the passing of this Act, then it certainly comes under the Act.
I do not think this language means what the hon.. gentleman intended it to mean, judging from this speech.
It means that this Act does not apply to a mortgage made before the passing of the Act unless it is renewed after the passing of the Act.
What do you mean by 'renewed'?

By signing or executing a renewal agreement to extend the time whereby the mortgagor agrees to keep the money for a further period, and the mortgagee consents that he shall keep it for a further period. If that is done after the passing of this Act, although it is the same mortgage, and the old mortgage has not been discharged, yet the fact of that agreement being signed, brings that old mortgage within the Act, and gives the mortgagor the privilege of the Act when that second due date comes round, or when the maturity of the mortgage is reached.

The hon. gentleman makes it clear what he means, but I do not think that this Bill makes it clear. I do not think a court would say that this language means what he says. ' Whenever any principal money, interest or other money secured by mortgage made, or renewed by reriewal or extension agreement.' Now if it is not made or renewed by renewal or extension agreement, then the court will say that this Act does not apply.
No it does not, of course.

You are enacting here that subsection 10 is to be affected by the contents of 10a. But we start, with a new
section. By these words you have to be entirely within all the qualifications of that definition before the Act can apply. I cannot grasp what it does mean. Speaking as a lawyer, I do not believe that a court would put upon it any such construction as my hon. friend thinks that a court would put upon it. I think that is a very much restricted operation. You begin by interfering with the rights of contract. Now, the first principle of construction that a court of law would put upon it, is to limit the qualification as much as possible. By the complication of these words you will cause the court to say: This does not apply. If there is no question about the extent of this Act, then the qualification is not to apply, because, as I have said, it is an interference with the rights of contract, and the courts will say that it must be strictly construed. Now, the mortgage must be made or renewed by renewal or extension agreement. What i,s that to cover? Is that to cover every little agreement that a man has made for extension of time for the payment of interest on certain conditions? We know very well that the principle is not always paid when it becomes due, and it may be that the man does not pay the interest when it becomes due. It may be an extension agreement has been made, and yet that little "extension agreement is only to apply perhaps to a few dollars of interest. Is this Act to apply then? Perhaps the mortgagor forgets to pay the insurance premium, and under the Short Form Mortgages Act of Ontario, if he forgets to pay the insurance premium, the mortgagee can pay that premium and by special enactment, not in the contract, not in the mortgage which the man and his wife have signed, but by virtue of an Act which becomes of the same effect as if it was included in the mortgage, the mortgagee has a right to add that insurance premium as so much principal to his mortgage principal. Now, if he forgets to pay that, and the mortgagee pays it, then the mortgagee says: Well, you did not provide for this premium, it is past due, and I will extend the time for payment; then that additional principal becomes such by virtue of a clause of the Act. That is an extension agreement, that extends the time for payment of part of the sum. I voted for this Bill, but I am not in favour of making legislation that is going to get every farmer into a lawsuit with the loan company. The farmer is not going to get any benefit from it, and he will have to risk perhaps his whole farm by carryinig a case to the Privy Council to find out how far we have power to enact this legislation. The provincial legislatures deal with these matters, and while I am prepared to go as far as we can in using our jurisdiction to remedy an evil, I want to be careful that we are not going to get

the borrower into such a position that he will be encouraged to go into a lawsuit with the loan company, and after he has lost his farm, will find out that the Act does not mean what my hon. friend thinks it means. I think that we ought to recast this section so that the leader of the opposition, myself and other members of this House can all understand it to mean exactly what the hon. gentleman does, because, I am inclined to say, that I cannot be sure if the court will put any such construction upon it as the proposer of the Bill does.

The object of the Bill is simply to provide for the case of a mortgage not being paid when due, or at the time to which it has been extended by agreement. I appreciate the objection which has been raised toy the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) and I think that if we would recast just the first three or four lines it would obviate all this difficulty. I would suggest that it might be recast in this way :
Whenever any principal money or other money secured by mortgage made after the passing of this Act or hereafter renewed by renewal or extension agreement thereof.

I appreciate the object which tl^e hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) has, but I am bound to say that the drafting of this Bill, including some of the expressions that the hon. gentleman proposes to retain, seems rather of a slangy description. I do not know the practice in other provinces, but in the province of Nova Scotia, I have never heard the expression: 'Extension agreement.' When that came up for construction before a court of that province some of the judges might say that they had heard of extension tables but that they had never heard the term * extension agreement ' before.
It is used in practice.
It is not used in my province.
It is quite common.
Is it common in statutes and legal documents.
It is very common in practice.
Is it used in legal documents?
Yes.
I have never heard it.
I have drawn up lots of documents containing it.
You might get over it by calling it an ' agreement to extend the time for payment.'
I suppose the Minister of Public Works will appreciate the suggestion that I have made.
I have never heard it called an extension agreement before, but I should think that you could say an ' agreement to extend the time for the payment of the principal money.'

Something of that kind so that we could have an intelligent idea of what it means. We might call it an extension agreement in debate if we desired to do so, but when we are framing a statute which has to be considered by the courts we should be more particular.

1.	What progress has been made in the generating of electric power from producer gas from peat?	,
2.	What is the process of preparing the peat?
3.	What is the price per ton of peat and how does its efficiency compare with coal?
4.	What horse-power can be generated daily in the experimental plant and at what cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
1.	The installing of the peat gas producer and gas engine, electric generator and switchboard was completed March 21, 1910. From this date to June 1, seven tests were made to determine the fuel consumption per brake horse-power hour. The peat used during these tests was that made some three years ago at the Victoria! Road Peat Bog, and, although the fuel consumption-that is, pounds of peat consumed per brake horse-power hour-was very satisfactory, being between 21 and 2i pounds, the peat proved unsuitable ori account of its dryness and the large percentage of ash, which is accounted for by the fact that the peat was dug from d shallow part of the bog, which contained sand.
From June to the present date the plant has not been operated on account of the installation of the laboratory for the com centration of iron ores and the gas analytical laboratory, which is indispensable in connection with the gas producer tests. The concentrating laboratory is completed and the gas analytical laboratory will be completed in the course of a week or ten days. During this period, on account of the above work, tests could not be carried on.
The official gas producer tests with the peat manufactured at the government peat bog will be further delayed for a month or six weeks by the installation of a new gas producer which is designed for using bituminous and lignite coal, and, it is confidently expected, peat. The operation of this new producer will be more simple and satisfactory than the one already installed.
The work of testing the peat manufactured at the government peat bog at Alfred will be begun immediately upon the installation of this new producer and the investigations to be made will cover the behaviour of peat in these two producers. The results will be published as soon as possible after the completion of the investigations.
2.	The process adopted at the government peat bog for the manufacture of peat for domestic and industrial purposes is. the Anrep process, fully described in the report on Peat and Lignite, written by Mr. E. Nystrom, and published and distributed about two years ago, and in Bulletin No. 4, soon to be distributed, which contains a full description of the process employed at Alfred, in addition to maps and illustrations.
In short, the process consists in feeding the peat dug by hand to a pulping mill, which thoroughly macerates the material. The product, after passing through this' mill, has the consistency of porridge, and

in this state the peat readily parts with its moisture. From the pulping mill the peat is conveyed by small cars to the drying field, where it is spread out to the required thickness and cut into blocks. The peat is left here until sufficiently dry for use. The daily capacity of the peat plant at the government peat bog is 25 tons per 10-hour day.
3.	Allowing 140 days for a season's operation of a plant such as above described, using manual labour for digging peat instead of mechanical excavators, the cost per ton of air-dried machine peat, including	interest	on capital invested, amortization, oil and repairs, is as follows:
Cost of fuel on the field	 $1.40
Cost	of	fuel	stored in shed	 1.65
loaded on car	 1.65
in stack	 1.70
By the employment of mechanical excavators and the manufacture of peat on a large scale, the cost of production per ton should be considerably less than the) figures here given.
3.	The efficiency of peat compared with good anthracite coal is: 1 -8 tons of air-dried peat is equivalent in heating value to one ton of coal.
4.	Sixty horse-power can be generated daily at the experimental plant.
The cost has not been finally calculated, since no complete adequate tests have as yet been made.
Friday, December 9, 1910.
